items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we want to rewrite [MATH: \log_3(4) - \log_3(6)] as a single logarithm. We can do this using the quotient rule.

Content:
The quotient rule is very similar to the product rule, except that this time we're dealing with the difference of two logarithms rather than the sum.

Content:
The quotient rule states that two logarithms which share a common base [MATH: \color{blue}n] satisfy
[MATH: \log_{\color{blue}n} (a) - \log_{\color{blue}n} (b) = \log_{\color{blue}n}\left(\dfrac a b\right) .]

Content:
So, we can use this rule to rewrite [MATH: \log_{\color{blue}3}(4) - \log_{\color{blue}3}(6)] as

Content:
[MATH: \log_{3} 4 − \log_{3} (6)|= \log_{3} ((4)/(6)); = \log_{3} ((2)/(3)).]

Content:
The quotient rule works exactly the same for the natural and common logarithms.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we want to rewrite [MATH: \log_3(4) - \log_3(6)] as a single logarithm. We can do this using the quotient rule.

Content:
The quotient rule is very similar to the product rule, except that this time we're dealing with the difference of two logarithms rather than the sum.

Content:
The quotient rule states that two logarithms which share a common base [MATH: \color{blue}n] satisfy
[MATH: \log_{\color{blue}n} (a) - \log_{\color{blue}n} (b) = \log_{\color{blue}n}\left(\dfrac a b\right) .]

Content:
So, we can use this rule to rewrite [MATH: \log_{\color{blue}3}(4) - \log_{\color{blue}3}(6)] as

Content:
[MATH: \log_{3} 4 − \log_{3} (6)|= \log_{3} ((4)/(6)); = \log_{3} ((2)/(3)).]

Content:
The quotient rule works exactly the same for the natural and common logarithms.
